extracted.intended_audience: state air agencies, owners/operators of affected EGUs, electric utilities, reliability authorities, and EPA reviewers
extracted.subtask_short: state plan submission for EGU guidelines
extracted.subtask_description: Requirements and procedures for state plan development, submission, EPA review, and related permitting implications under the EPA's emission guidelines for existing electric generating units (EGUs). Covers timelines, documentation, coordination with reliability authorities, state plan revisions, EPA actions, Federal plan triggers, and NSR/BACT considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: EGU deactivation reporting and documentation requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Operators of EGUs that plan to permanently cease operation must provide an initial notice to the relevant reliability authority of the deactivation date and submit an official retirement filing (or equivalent) made to the EGU's reliability authority; for remaining years prior to permanent cessation the operator must submit annual status reports; and EGUs committing to permanently cease operation by January 1, 2032 must submit a final report within 6 months following committed closure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supporting regulatory documents must be provided, including correspondence and official filings with relevant RTOs, ISOs, balancing authorities, PUCs, reliability authorities; any deactivation-related reliability assessments by RTO/ISO; filings with the SEC or investor notices (e.g., 10-K/10-Q) referencing EGU plans; integrated resource plans and PUC orders referring to or approving deactivation; any reliability analyses developed in response to deactivation notification; notifications from reliability authorities that the EGU may be needed notwithstanding intent to deactivate; and any notifications altering timing of deactivation. Annual reports must document (1) progress on process steps identified in the initial report, (2) supporting regulatory documents demonstrating progress, and (3) regulatory documents and SEC filings issued since the prior report. Final report should document actions taken after cessation to ensure permanence, including regulatory filings or decommissioning plans.

rubrics_metrics.name: State plan submission deadline (24 months)
rubrics_metrics.description: States must submit state plans 24 months after publication of the final emission guidelines in the Federal Register.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA is superseding subpart Ba's default 18-month timeline and finalizes 24 months to accommodate additional coordination needs (e.g., with reliability authorities). The 24-month period reflects EPA's judgment about the minimum administrative time reasonably necessary for states and owners/operators to coordinate and develop plans consistent with broader power sector needs while proceeding expeditiously to protect public health.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordination with reliability authorities and multi-stakeholder consultation
rubrics_metrics.description: State plan development requires significant analysis, consultation, and coordination among states, utilities, reliability authorities (ISOs/RTOs/balancing authorities), and owners/operators of affected EGUs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States' plan development may have to integrate decision-making across relevant air agencies, ISOs/RTOs, PUCs, and other authorities; EPA expects states and affected EGUs to coordinate with operators as they update IRPs and proceed through necessary processes with PUCs and reliability authorities. This coordination informed EPA's determination of an appropriate submission timeline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment of EGUs to subcategories and legal instruments at submission
rubrics_metrics.description: States must assign each affected EGU to a subcategory in their state plans and have in place all legal instruments necessary to implement the requirements for that subcategory by the time of state plan submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because switching subcategories may prevent an affected EGU from meeting new compliance obligations without considerable lead time, states should identify subcategory assignments at submission to provide regulatory certainty. If an EGU wishes to switch subcategories later, the state must submit a plan revision sufficiently in advance of the compliance date to permit EPA review and action.

rubrics_metrics.name: No dual-path/multi-path standards of performance approach
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA is not finalizing an approach that would allow coal-fired steam generating units to have multiple different standards of performance (dual-path or multi-path) submitted to EPA based on potential inclusion in multiple subcategories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the final guidelines include only two subcategories for coal-fired affected EGUs (and not the previously proposed additional subcategories), the dual-path approach is not finalized. States must submit a single standard of performance assignment per EGU; changes require a plan revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: State plan revisions: process, requirements, and enforceability
rubrics_metrics.description: States may submit revised state plans to the EPA; revisions are generally subject to the same requirements as initial submissions, including meaningful engagement; EPA reviews revisions under the same criteria as initial plans; approved initial plan requirements remain federally enforceable until superseded by an EPA-approved revision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State plan revisions must satisfy subpart Ba requirements and meaningful engagement. EPA notes it is not finalizing a cutoff date that would establish a temporary moratorium on plan submissions prior to the first compliance date, but also cautions that revisions submitted very late (e.g., after November 1, 2028) may not provide sufficient time for EPA review before the first compliance date (Jan 1, 2030 for certain subcategories).

rubrics_metrics.name: EPA completeness and review timelines and possible determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must determine completeness of a state plan submission within 60 days of receipt and must take final action on a submission within 12 months of it being deemed complete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If EPA fails to make a completeness determination within 60 days, the submission is deemed complete by operation of law. Upon completeness, EPA has 12 months to act and may fully approve, fully disapprove, partially approve/partially disapprove, or conditionally approve a state plan submission. Approved components become federally enforceable.

rubrics_metrics.name: No automatic extension of compliance dates based on EPA review timing
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA will not provide automatic extensions of compliance dates for affected EGUs if EPA does not meet its 12-month deadline for plan approval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA believes making compliance dates contingent on EPA's action date would create uncertainty and could delay emissions reductions; therefore, review timelines in subpart Ba remain governing and compliance dates will not be automatically extended due to EPA review delays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal plan triggers and promulgation timing
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA's obligation to promulgate a Federal plan is triggered where a state does not submit a plan by the deadline, where EPA determines a submission does not meet completeness criteria and the submission period has elapsed, or where EPA disapproves a state's plan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subpart Ba gives EPA 12 months from the state plan submission due date to promulgate a Federal plan where a state failed to submit; otherwise the 12-month period starts from when the plan is deemed incomplete or from the date of EPA disapproval. A Federal plan will prescribe standards of performance of the same stringency as required by these emission guidelines and require compliance as expeditiously as practicable but no later than the final compliance date. Upon application by an owner/operator, EPA may provide for less stringent performance or longer compliance schedules following the same processes/criteria that apply to states' RULOF standards. EPA must conduct meaningful engagement with pertinent stakeholders prior to promulgating a Federal plan.

rubrics_metrics.name: NSR program applicability and state/federal roles
rubrics_metrics.description: NSR preconstruction permitting applies to new construction and modifications of stationary sources; states have primary responsibility for issuing NSR permits and can customize programs within EPA limits; EPA's role is to approve state program regulations and review/comment on permits to assure consistency with EPA rules, the SIP, and the CAA. When a state lacks authority, EPA issues NSR permits or delegates authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal NSR rules for state permitting authorities are at 40 CFR 51.160–51.166. Where delegated, EPA regional offices or the EPA will perform permitting. NSR applicability is pollutant-specific: a source may need major and/or minor NSR permits depending on pollutant thresholds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinctions among PSD, NNSR, and minor NSR permitting requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: For major NSR: PSD permits apply in attainment/unclassifiable areas and must include BACT for each pollutant subject to PSD; NNSR applies in nonattainment areas and requires LAER and offsets; minor NSR applies to projects below major thresholds and lacks a statutory minimum control technology requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PSD permits must demonstrate emissions will not cause or contribute to NAAQS violations or exceed PSD increments; BACT may be used to make this demonstration. NNSR sources must provide or purchase offsets to compensate for increases. Minor NSR gives permitting authorities more flexibility since no minimum control tech standard is specified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public participation and environmental justice considerations in NSR permitting
rubrics_metrics.description: Permitting authorities must provide opportunity for public hearing and allow submission of written/oral comments on air quality impact, alternatives, control technology required, and 'other appropriate considerations.' Environmental justice considerations can be considered, and permitting authorities have discretion to enhance engagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EAB has encouraged permit issuers to examine plausible claims of disproportionate impacts. EPA guidance and EAB decisions do not require integrating EJ into specific components like BACT, but practice has been to conduct largely freestanding EJ analyses for PSD permits. States implementing NSR under an EPA-approved SIP have discretion to consider EJ and adopt additional permitting requirements; some state laws require EJ consideration. Authorities can enhance participation by extending comment periods, holding multiple public meetings, providing translation services, or meeting with community groups before draft permits are issued.

rubrics_metrics.name: BACT control-technology review and five-step 'top-down' approach
rubrics_metrics.description: In conducting a BACT analysis for PSD permits, permitting authorities often apply EPA's five-step 'top-down' approach: identify all available control options with potential practical application; eliminate technically infeasible options; rank remaining options from most to least effective; evaluate energy, environmental, economic, and other costs and eliminate options not achievable; select the most effective remaining option as BACT.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The BACT review evaluates emission reductions and the energy/environmental/economic/other costs of each technology. While BACT should generally not be applied to regulate the permit applicant's purpose/objective or require fundamentally redefining the source, permitting authorities have discretion to consider options that would change aspects of facility design and may conduct a broader BACT analysis if desired. BACT cannot be less stringent than any applicable NSPS standard of performance.
